definition.text: A total allowable catch system caps the catch of a whole fishery: fishers may fish when and how they like until the quota is met, then fishing stops until the next season.

facts.text: A TAC does not remove the underlying competition among fishers for the fish.
TACs often produce overcapitalization of the industry and races between boat crews to land fish before the quota runs out.
In the Alaskan halibut fishery the race became so extreme that the season shrank to a single 24-hour dash, and perishable fish were landed in a clump.
The EU Common Fisheries Policy sets TACs per species and ICES area, yearly or two-yearly, and gives each country a quota from its traditional percentage share.

definition.text: The race to fish is the scramble to catch as much as possible during short open seasons, which catch shares are designed to end.

facts.text: Early management set a fishing season whose length tracked how abundant the stock was.
With catch shares, fishers can schedule trips as they like, boom-and-bust market cycles fade, and fishing in hazardous weather becomes unnecessary.
Under a total allowable catch each boat competes to land fish before the quota is reached, which pushes owners toward overcapitalization.
In Alaskan halibut the race cut the season to one 24-hour dash; the resource-economics text says ITQs later ended overcapitalization and spread the catch over time.

contested_note: Commentators disagree on whether the policy harmed stocks or merely failed to reverse a decline that predated it.
title: Common Fisheries Policy

definition.text: The Common Fisheries Policy is the European Union's fisheries policy: it sets catch quotas, gives member states access to one another's exclusive economic zones and manages sustainable fishing in the EU's zone.

facts.text: Member states may implement the common principles through licences, limited entry or individual fishing quota, and regulations cover gear and closed areas.
Enforcement is left to member states, with a community inspection service checking them.
The 2013 reform, in force from 1 January 2014, was meant to protect endangered stocks and end discards, with maximum sustainable yield to apply from 2015.
Critics say per-species quotas force fish to be thrown overboard dead, and that its centralised top-down command-and-control approach should give way to participatory governance.
A 2010 study traced stock depletion to mismanagement long before the policy, with British catch rates down 94% over 118 years.
